def solve_all(text):
    data = text.split()
    t = int(data[0])
    pos = 1
    out = []

widget.solution:
def solve_all(text):
    data = text.split()
    t = int(data[0])
    pos = 1
    out = []
    for _ in range(t):
        n = int(data[pos])
        pos += 1
        seen = set()
        for s in data[pos:pos + n]:
            seen.add(s)
        pos += n
        out.append(len(seen))
    return out

Only call `sys.setrecursionlimit(10**6)`
options.why: You raised the limit. It works in this app's Pyodide, which ran a million frames in our test. On some judges, deep recursion still crashes the interpreter.

options.why: You halved the depth. A line of 100,000 still needs 50,000 frames.

hints.text: What grows with the length of the line?
Each `dfs` call waits for the next one: 100,000 frames deep.
An explicit stack keeps the pending nodes in a list, so depth costs memory, not frames.

feedback.correct: An explicit stack never hits a depth limit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Choose the fix that removes deep recursion.

explain.text: A list used as a stack holds the nodes still to visit, so depth is just list length. Raising the limit can help, but an explicit stack works on every judge. In C++, check `int` overflow at the same step.

quiz.prose: In C++, you sum $n = 2 \cdot 10^5$ values, each up to $10^9$, into an `int`.
quiz.question: What happens on the largest test?

options.text: It overflows: the sum can reach $2 \cdot 10^{14}$
Nothing: an `int` holds any sum of `int`s
options.why: You assumed the sum stays in range. A 32-bit `int` stops at 2,147,483,647.

options.text: It is too slow
options.why: Adding $2 \cdot 10^5$ numbers takes microseconds. The problem is the type.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the largest sum with an `int`'s limit.

explain.text: $2 \cdot 10^5 \cdot 10^9 = 2 \cdot 10^{14}$, while an `int` holds at most $2^{31} - 1 \approx 2.1 \cdot 10^9$. A `long long` holds up to about $9.2 \cdot 10^{18}$.
